claims.text: Phase-selective recrystallization can simultaneously increase strength and ductility in eutectic high-entropy alloys.
The initial eutectic high-entropy alloy contains FCC and B2 phases.
The proposed intervention consists of two cycles of 30% cold rolling followed by annealing at 1200 °C for 20 minutes and water quenching.
The intervention produces a phase-selectively recrystallized microstructure.
During deformation, local von Mises strain in the FCC phase can be up to six times that in the B2 phase.
The FCC–B2 strain disparity caused by phase-selective recrystallization leads to improved strength and ductility.
The phase-selectively recrystallized alloy should achieve approximately 33% uniform elongation.
The phase-selectively recrystallized alloy should achieve an engineering ultimate tensile strength approaching 2.2 GPa.
The as-cast baseline has approximately 14% fracture true strain.
The as-cast baseline has approximately 1390 MPa fracture true stress.
The expected properties apply to quasi-static uniaxial tensile testing at room temperature and an initial strain rate of 1 × 10^-3 s^-1.
The process may not be effective for every eutectic high-entropy alloy or under different testing conditions.
The exact mechanisms by which phase-selective recrystallization improves strength and ductility are not fully understood.
A comparison of alloys with and without phase-selective recrystallization can test the hypothesis.
Failure to obtain significant improvements in both strength and ductility relative to the as-cast alloy would falsify the hypothesis.
